check.x: Professionalism
Washes hands, introduces self and role, confirms Rachel's name, and explains and gains consent before examining.
Warm and unhurried: expresses sorrow for the loss of her baby and acknowledges her fear as understandable.
Uses plain language and explains or avoids jargon such as CTG and liquor.
History
Takes a focused history of the reduced movements:

kids.x: Usual pattern of movements and when they changed [reduced since about 6 pm yesterday]
When the baby last moved and what she has tried [a few weak flutters; a cold drink and lying on her left side did not help]
Bleeding, fluid loss, abdominal pain or tightenings, and trauma [all nil]
Fever or flu-like illness, as listeria and other infections can harm the baby [nil]
Pre-eclampsia symptoms: headache, visual disturbance, upper abdominal pain, new swelling [nil]

check.x: Takes an obstetric history and summarises it correctly:

kids.x: Miscarriage at 9 weeks, and a stillbirth at 39 weeks two years ago with no cause found other than a small placenta
States G3 and TPAL correctly: T1 (a term stillbirth counts as a term birth), P0, A1 (miscarriage before 20 weeks), L0

check.x: Explores risk factors in this pregnancy:

kids.x: Gestational diabetes, diet-controlled, diagnosed at 27 weeks
Aspirin 150 mg at night from 13 weeks
Growth scan normal at 32 weeks, and blood pressure normal this pregnancy
Smoking, alcohol and drugs, and sleep position [non-smoker, none, sometimes goes to sleep on her back]

check.x: Screens mood, sleep and support, including thoughts of self-harm [anxious, sleeping poorly, no self-harm thoughts, supportive husband].
Explores her ideas, concerns and expectations, including why she waited before coming in.
Examination
Asks for maternal observations and a urine dipstick, and repeats the blood pressure.
Examines the abdomen: inspection, symphysis-fundal height compared with dates [35 cm], lie and presentation [longitudinal, cephalic] and uterine tenderness.
Listens to the fetal heart with a handheld Doppler [142 bpm, regular].
Looks for signs of pre-eclampsia: reflexes, clonus, epigastric or right upper quadrant tenderness and oedema.
Interpretation
Interprets the observations and urinalysis as normal: normal blood pressure, no proteinuria, afebrile and a normal glucose, so no sign of pre-eclampsia or infection.
Interprets the CTG as normal: baseline 140 bpm, variability 10 bpm, accelerations present, no decelerations.
States that a normal CTG is reassuring now but does not exclude a baby at risk, for example from growth restriction or a poorly functioning placenta.

Identifies her risk factors for stillbirth: previous stillbirth with a small placenta, previous pre-eclampsia, gestational diabetes, sometimes going to sleep on her back and the delay before coming in.
Management
Arranges an ultrasound today to check the baby's growth and the amount of fluid around the baby, and review by the registrar or obstetric team before she goes home.
Answers "Will it be all right?" honestly: does not promise a good outcome, but promises that her worries will always be taken seriously.
Aspirin: explains it lowers the risk of pre-eclampsia and is stopped at 36 weeks, so she should now stop it, and confirms the plan with the registrar rather than guessing.
Answers the food question:

kids.x: Listeria is usually a mild illness for her but can seriously harm the baby
Avoid cold deli meats and soft cheeses such as brie and camembert, with a written food list
Avoiding these foods lowers the risk but cannot remove it; yesterday's baguette is most likely low risk and needs no test while she is well

check.x: Plans ongoing care with the obstetric team: closer monitoring and the timing of birth given the previous stillbirth, and offers perinatal mental health support.
Summarises the plan, checks her understanding and asks if she has other questions.
Safety netting
If movements reduce or change again, come in straight away, at any time of day or night, without waiting until morning; she is never wasting anyone's time.
Go to sleep on her side, not her back, for every sleep, including daytime naps.
Come in promptly for a fever or flu-like illness (listeria can show up weeks after eating), or for bleeding, fluid loss, abdominal pain, headache or changes in vision.
Explains her later health risks and the follow-up:

kids.x: Pre-eclampsia and gestational diabetes both raise her later risk of heart disease; pre-eclampsia also raises the risk of high blood pressure, stroke and kidney disease
Gestational diabetes greatly raises the risk of type 2 diabetes: a glucose tolerance test 6 to 12 weeks after the birth, then regular glucose checks
Regular GP review of blood pressure, weight and cholesterol

desc: This station involves a focused history and examination of a woman at 36 weeks with reduced fetal movements after a previous stillbirth, then interpreting her observations and CTG, explaining honestly what a normal trace means, planning further assessment, answering her questions about aspirin, food safety and later health, and safety-netting.
diagnosis: Reduced fetal movements with normal cardiotocograph
explain:
Reduced fetal movements

Women should be encouraged to learn their baby's usual pattern of movements and to report any reduction promptly, at any time of day or night. Assessment is a focused history (the change in movements, bleeding, fluid loss, pain, infection and pre-eclampsia symptoms, and risk factors), maternal observations and urinalysis, abdominal palpation with symphysis-fundal height, auscultation of the fetal heart, and a CTG. Previous stillbirth, growth restriction, pre-eclampsia, diabetes and going to sleep on the back are recognised risk factors. The Safer Baby Bundle supports awareness of movements, side sleeping from 28 weeks, smoking cessation, growth surveillance and decisions about the timing of birth.

Interpreting the results

Rachel's blood pressure, urinalysis, temperature and glucose are normal, so there is no sign of pre-eclampsia or infection. Her CTG is normal: a baseline of 140 bpm (normal range 110 to 160), variability of 10 bpm (normal 6 to 25), accelerations and no decelerations. A normal CTG is reassuring about the baby's condition now but does not exclude the risk of a poor outcome, so with her risk factors an ultrasound to assess fetal growth and amniotic fluid volume should be arranged today, with obstetric review before she goes home.

Communicating after a previous stillbirth

  • Acknowledge the loss and validate the anxiety. Do not say "it will be fine".
  • Be honest about uncertainty, but promise to take her concerns seriously and to respond each time she presents.
  • Plan surveillance and the timing of birth together with the obstetric team, and offer perinatal mental health support. Screen for depression and anxiety and ask about self-harm.

TPAL

T: term births (37 weeks or more). P: preterm births (20 weeks to under 37 weeks). A: pregnancies lost before 20 weeks. L: living children. A multiple pregnancy counts once. A stillbirth at term counts as a term birth. Rachel is G3, with T1 P0 A1 L0, and her current pregnancy adds to gravidity but not to parity until she gives birth.

Listeria and food safety

Listeria is usually a mild illness in the mother but can cause miscarriage, stillbirth, preterm birth or severe neonatal infection. Advise avoiding cold deli meats, pâté and soft or semi-soft cheeses such as brie and camembert, along with the other high-risk foods in the national guidance, and give a written list. Avoidance lowers the risk but cannot remove it. A well woman who ate a high-risk food needs no test, but any fever or flu-like illness in pregnancy should prompt early contact with the maternity unit, as illness can appear weeks after exposure.

Aspirin for pre-eclampsia prevention

Low-dose aspirin (100 to 150 mg at night) started before 16 weeks lowers the risk of pre-eclampsia in women at higher risk, such as those with previous pre-eclampsia. In line with current Australian guidance (SOMANZ 2023), it is stopped at 36 weeks, or earlier if birth is imminent. Rachel is at 36+2, so the correct advice is that it should now be stopped. Because she is unsure, the candidate should confirm the plan with the obstetric team and not rely on memory.

Safety netting and later health

  • Come in straight away, at any hour, if movements reduce or change again, and go to sleep on her side for every sleep.
  • Come in promptly for fever, bleeding, fluid loss, abdominal pain, headache or visual changes.
  • Pregnancy acts as a cardiometabolic stress test. Pre-eclampsia and gestational diabetes both predict higher later cardiovascular risk. Pre-eclampsia also raises the later risk of chronic hypertension, stroke and chronic kidney disease.
  • Gestational diabetes greatly raises the risk of type 2 diabetes. A glucose tolerance test is recommended 6 to 12 weeks after birth, followed by glucose screening every 1 to 3 years, with GP review of blood pressure, weight, lipids and lifestyle.
focus: Antenatal visit: food advice, reduced fetal movements, anxiety after stillbirth and later health risks
guide:
In Part 1, the examiner gives findings from the Exam findings only when the candidate says what they would examine. Rachel raises her food and aspirin questions near the end of Part 1; the candidate may answer them then or in Part 2, and both count. If the candidate asks for an ultrasound, a slot is available in the unit today. A high-performing candidate takes a focused history that clarifies the change in movements and screens for bleeding, fluid loss, infection and pre-eclampsia, states her obstetric history correctly (G3, T1 P0 A1 L0), screens mood including self-harm, and examines the abdomen, the fetal heart and for signs of pre-eclampsia. In Part 2 they interpret the observations and CTG as normal but explain that a normal trace is not a guarantee, arrange an ultrasound today and obstetric review, recognise that aspirin should now be stopped and confirm this with the registrar, give accurate listeria advice, and tell her to come in at any hour if movements change, to sleep on her side, and what her pre-eclampsia and gestational diabetes mean later in life.

A borderline candidate takes a reasonable history but misses the obstetric summary, the mood screen or the fetal heart. They may say the baby is fine because the trace is normal, promise that everything will be all right, tell her to keep taking aspirin, give vague food advice, or give vague safety netting such as "come back if you are worried".
patient:
Role: You are Rachel Bennett, a 34-year-old primary school teacher (on leave), 36 weeks and 2 days into your third pregnancy, in the maternity day assessment unit. You are not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander. The examiner gives examination findings from the Exam findings when the candidate says what they would examine.

Demeanour: Pale, tearful and tense. You sit forward, hold your abdomen and keep checking the clock. You speak quickly, and calm a little if the candidate is warm and unhurried.

Opening line: "I haven't felt the baby move much since last night. I'm so scared it's happening again."

Reduced movements (give only when asked):

  • The baby is usually very active, especially after dinner and when you lie down in the evening.
  • Since about 6 pm yesterday you have felt only a few weak flutters. This morning you felt perhaps two small movements.
  • You tried a cold drink and lying on your left side. This did not help much.
  • No vaginal bleeding, no fluid leaking, no abdominal pain or tightenings, no fall or injury to your abdomen.
  • No fever, chills, sore throat or flu-like illness at any point in the pregnancy.
  • No headache, problems with your vision, pain under the ribs or new swelling.
  • You usually go to sleep on your side, but some nights you fall asleep on your back, and you often wake on your back.
  • You waited about 18 hours before coming in because you did not want to "waste anyone's time". If asked, say you are sorry you did not come sooner.

Obstetric history:

  • This is your third pregnancy.
  • First pregnancy: miscarriage at 9 weeks.
  • Second pregnancy, two years ago: pre-eclampsia (high blood pressure and protein in the urine) diagnosed at 37 weeks. Your son was stillborn at 39 weeks, before the planned induction. No cause was found other than a small placenta.
  • You have no living children. If asked, say: "I've never taken a baby home."
  • If the candidate gives a summary such as G3, T1 P0 A1 L0, you do not need to comment.

This pregnancy:

  • Single baby, conceived naturally. Regular antenatal visits.
  • Aspirin 150 mg every night, started at 13 weeks because of the pre-eclampsia last time.
  • Gestational diabetes diagnosed at 27 weeks on a glucose tolerance test, managed with diet only. Home sugar readings have been fine.
  • Growth scan at 32 weeks was normal. Blood pressure has been normal this pregnancy.

Medical history: nil else. No mental health diagnosis before the stillbirth. Medicines: aspirin 150 mg at night and a pregnancy multivitamin with iodine. Allergies: none.

Social history: you live with your husband, Daniel, who is very supportive. Non-smoker. No alcohol or drugs since conceiving.

Mood (give if asked): very anxious since the stillbirth and sleeping poorly; you count movements through the night. You feel low at times but have no thoughts of harming yourself. You have not seen a counsellor this pregnancy and would like help if offered.

Ideas, concerns and expectations: you are terrified the baby will die like your son. You want someone to check the baby properly. You hope to be told everything is fine so you can go home.

During the examination: if the candidate listens to the baby's heartbeat, ask "Is that the heartbeat? Is it normal?" Say you feel a small movement while your abdomen is being examined.

Questions to raise near the end of Part 1 (the candidate may answer them now or in Part 2):

  1. "Yesterday Daniel bought me a ham and brie baguette. I ate half before I remembered I'm not supposed to. Should I be worried?" (You have no fever or flu-like symptoms.)
  2. "I take my aspirin every night. I think the midwife said something about stopping it at some point. Should I keep taking it until the baby comes?" (You took your last dose last night.)

In Part 2, if the candidate speaks to you: if told the trace is normal, ask "So the baby is fine? Can I go home?" If told the baby is definitely fine, become more distressed: "They said that last time too." If the candidate explains that the trace cannot guarantee everything is fine and offers an ultrasound, accept with relief. Ask "Is it going to be all right this time? Please just tell me it will be." If there is time, ask "I had pre-eclampsia last time and sugar diabetes this time. Does that mean anything for my health later on?" If the candidate does not say when to come back, ask "What if it happens again when I get home?"

If the candidate uses jargon (CTG, liquor, EFW, OGTT, listeriosis), interrupt and ask what it means.
points: A normal CTG for reduced fetal movements is reassuring but not a guarantee, so offer an ultrasound and advise her to come in again straight away, at any hour, if movements change.
After a previous stillbirth, acknowledge the loss and validate the anxiety. Do not promise a good outcome, but promise to take her worries seriously and plan monitoring and support together.
TPAL records term births, preterm births, pregnancies lost before 20 weeks, and living children. A term stillbirth counts as a term birth.
Advise avoiding cold deli meats and soft cheeses because of listeria. Avoidance lowers but does not remove the risk, and a fever or flu-like illness needs prompt review.
Low-dose aspirin for pre-eclampsia prevention is stopped at 36 weeks (or earlier if birth is imminent). Confirm the plan with the obstetric team.

Pre-eclampsia and gestational diabetes both raise later cardiovascular risk. Pre-eclampsia also raises the risk of hypertension, stroke and chronic kidney disease, and gestational diabetes greatly raises the risk of type 2 diabetes, hence the postpartum glucose tolerance test and ongoing screening.
refs: Australian Government Department of Health. Clinical Practice Guidelines: Pregnancy Care. 2020 edition.
Centre of Research Excellence in Stillbirth. Clinical practice guideline for the care of women with decreased fetal movements for women with a singleton pregnancy from 28 weeks' gestation. 2019.
Centre of Research Excellence in Stillbirth. Safer Baby Bundle Handbook and Resource Guide: working together to reduce stillbirth. 2019.
Perinatal Society of Australia and New Zealand (PSANZ). Clinical Practice Guideline for Care Around Stillbirth and Neonatal Death.
Society of Obstetric Medicine of Australia and New Zealand (SOMANZ). Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline. 2023.
Queensland Clinical Guidelines. Gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM).
stem: You are the junior doctor in the maternity day assessment unit of a metropolitan public hospital. Rachel Bennett, a 34-year-old woman who is 36 weeks and 2 days pregnant, has come in because she has felt her baby moving less since yesterday evening. The midwife has recorded her observations and started a CTG. The registrar has asked you to see Rachel while they review another patient.
tasks: Take a focused history from Rachel, including her obstetric history, and perform a focused examination, telling the examiner what you are examining and why (10 minutes).

The examiner will give you Rachel's observations, urinalysis and CTG. Interpret them, then outline your management approach, including your answers to Rachel's questions, and your safety netting (5 minutes).
title: Reduced movements and worry after a previous stillbirth

part2.lead: Here are Rachel's observations and urinalysis, and her 40-minute CTG.

handover.label: Maternal observations and urinalysis
handover.result: Urine dipstick at 12:20: protein nil, glucose nil, blood nil, leucocytes nil, nitrites nil.
handover.model:
Read: every observation is normal for 36 weeks. BP 116/72 mmHg on two readings 10 minutes apart (well below 140/90), HR 84 (normal; the resting heart rate runs 10 to 20 beats higher in late pregnancy), RR 16, SpO2 99% on room air, afebrile at 36.8 °C and capillary glucose 5.1 mmol/L. The dipstick shows no protein, glucose, leucocytes or nitrites.

Meaning: no sign of pre-eclampsia despite her history, no sign of infection (listeriosis usually brings a fever or flu-like illness) and nothing to suggest her diet-controlled gestational diabetes is out of control (her home readings have been fine). Nothing here explains the reduced movements, and Rachel's observations say nothing about the baby.

What it changes: nothing urgent for Rachel herself. The baby is assessed by the CTG and an ultrasound today, and her blood pressure and urine are checked again at every visit because of her previous pre-eclampsia.

rows.note: BP repeated after 10 minutes; urine dipstick done

handover.label: CTG (40 minutes)
handover.result:
Antenatal CTG at 36 weeks 2 days, 12:10 to 12:50 (40 minutes), paper speed 1 cm/min. Indication: reduced fetal movements; previous stillbirth. Rachel semi-recumbent with a left tilt.

FeatureFinding
SignalGood throughout, no loss of contact; fetal heart clearly separate from the maternal pulse (84/min)
Baseline rate140 bpm
Baseline variability10 bpm
AccelerationsFour in 40 minutes (two in each 20-minute period), each rising at least 15 bpm above the baseline for at least 15 seconds
DecelerationsNone
Uterine activityNo contractions
Fetal movementsRachel pressed the event marker 3 times for small movements, 2 of them with an acceleration
handover.model:
Read: a 40-minute antenatal CTG with a good signal: baseline 140 bpm (normal 110 to 160), variability 10 bpm (normal 6 to 25), four accelerations of at least 15 bpm for 15 seconds (at least two in each 20 minutes), no decelerations and no contractions. Every feature is normal, so by the RANZCOG criteria this is a normal antenatal CTG.

Meaning: a normal CTG means a low probability of fetal compromise at the time of the trace. It is a snapshot: it does not measure growth or how well the placenta works, so it cannot exclude growth restriction or placental insufficiency in a woman with a previous stillbirth with a small placenta, previous pre-eclampsia and gestational diabetes, who also sometimes goes to sleep on her back and waited 18 hours to come in.

What it changes: no need to expedite birth today, but she does not simply go home: an ultrasound today for fetal growth, liquor volume and umbilical artery Doppler, and review by the registrar before she leaves, with a plan for surveillance and the timing of birth. Rachel is told honestly that the trace is reassuring now but is not a guarantee.

ask: What do the observations, urinalysis and CTG show, and how reassuring are they for Rachel?
What is your assessment of Rachel's risk, and what else would you want to exclude?
What is your management plan today? Include what you tell Rachel about her aspirin and the baguette she ate.
What safety netting and follow-up would you give, including what her pre-eclampsia and gestational diabetes mean for her health later in life?
